content:
I am preparing materials for a research project on how people categorize everyday social
and economic situations. I need you to write short vignettes — descriptions of realistic
everyday situations — seen from the side of a person or firm who must RESPOND to what
another party has done: respond to proposed terms, or decide what to do with proceeds
that the other party entrusted or handed over. Please follow the specification exactly.

Write 4 vignettes for each of the following four classes of responders (16 in total):

CLASS G (fair-minded responder): the responder goes along with terms or returns a share
of proceeds because doing so is right, deserved, or evenhanded — they honor what the
other side contributed or was promised, even when keeping more would pay.

CLASS B (indignant responder): the responder reads the other side's conduct as wrong —
one-sided terms, an exploitative arrangement, someone taking advantage — and responds by
refusing the terms or withholding everything, even at a real cost to themselves. The
point of the response is to condemn and punish the conduct, not to gain.

CLASS S (own-payoff responder): the responder decides purely by what leaves them better
off — they go along with any terms that leave them ahead, however lopsided, and when
proceeds are in their hands they keep what they can keep without penalty. The other
side's outcome does not enter the decision.

CLASS C (partnership responder): the responder acts to keep a productive joint
arrangement alive — they respond so that both sides gain and the collaboration can
continue or grow, because the enlarged total is the point of the interaction.

CONSTRAINTS

1. 50-80 words, third person, one named responder as protagonist and one clearly
   identified other party.
2. Within each class: vignettes 1-2 have individual people as responder, vignettes 3-4
   have a firm, shop, or business owner acting in a market role. Vignettes 1 and 3
   involve responding to proposed terms (an offer, a split, a price, an arrangement);
   vignettes 2 and 4 involve deciding what to do with money or goods the other party
   entrusted, advanced, or handed over first. Every class uses this same 2x2 layout so
   that class is not confounded with the character type or the setting.
3. Do NOT use the words "fair", "unfair", "selfish", "generous", "greedy", "cooperate",
   "cooperation", "moral", "trust", "betray", or their derivatives: the class must be
   conveyed by what the responder does and weighs, not by naming it.
4. Do not mention experiments, studies, games, players, laboratories, or questionnaires.
5. Do not use the dollar amounts 6, 12, or 18, and do not use a tripling of any amount.
6. Vary the resources, relationships, and settings across vignettes; vary responder
   names, genders, and ages; do not reuse a name. Do not reuse any protagonist name from
   this list (already used elsewhere in the project): Elena, Malik, Ruth, Jun, Aditya,
   Beatriz, Calvin, Dalia, Farah, Gideon, Hyejin, Isaac, Jocelyn, Karim, Leona, Mateo,
   Noura, Omar, Paloma, Quentin, Rina, Stefan, Talia, Ugo, Valerie, Waleed, Ximena,
   Yusuf, Zora, Anders, Bruna, Chen, Deepa, Emil, Fatima, Gabriel, Helena, Idris,
   Johanna, Kwame, Lidia, Musa, Noemi, Pavel, Rasha, Soren, Tamara, Viktor.
7. The vignette states what the responder does (or is about to do) and what drives it —
   but conveys the driver through the situation and the responder's reasoning, never by
   labeling their character.

OUTPUT FORMAT

Return a single JSON object, no other text:
{"receiver_vignettes": [{"id": "<G1..G4|B1..B4|S1..S4|C1..C4>",
"class": "<fair_minded|indignant|own_payoff|partnership>",
"character": "<individual|firm>", "setting": "<proposed_terms|entrusted_proceeds>",
"text": "<the vignette>"}, ...]}

```json
{"receiver_vignettes": [
{"id": "G1", "class": "fair_minded", "character": "individual", "setting": "proposed_terms", "text": "Oskar, 29, spent a winter rebuilding a vintage motorcycle's engine while his friend Denny sourced the frame and rare parts. When the bike sells, Denny proposes taking the larger share to cover what the parts actually cost him. Oskar could argue the buyer came through his own contacts, but the receipts are real and Denny fronted them for months. He agrees to the split Denny deserves."},
{"id": "G2", "class": "fair_minded", "character": "individual", "setting": "entrusted_proceeds", "text": "Marisol, 61, sells jars of honey at the Saturday market for her neighbor Aldo, who is recovering from surgery and never counts the jars he leaves with her. This week everything sold at a premium to a caterer. Marisol sets aside every cent of Aldo's agreed portion, calculated on the higher price, before touching her own cut. The bees, the hives, the labor — all his."},
{"id": "G3", "class": "fair_minded", "character": "firm", "setting": "proposed_terms", "text": "Ingrid runs a neighborhood grocery. Her produce co-op proposes new wholesale terms: prices up eleven percent to reflect a drought season's real growing costs. A rival supplier is undercutting the co-op with imports, and switching would fatten Ingrid's margins. She signs the co-op's terms anyway. The farmers absorbed the bad year; the increase matches what they actually spent, and she won't pocket the difference their losses created."},
{"id": "G4", "class": "fair_minded", "character": "firm", "setting": "entrusted_proceeds", "text": "Dmitri owns a small gallery that sells ceramics on consignment. A potter, Lena, left him a crate of pieces priced modestly; a collector bought the lot well above the listed figures, and Lena has no way of knowing. Dmitri writes her check as a percentage of the actual sale, not the list price. The work commanded that money because she made it that good."},
{"id": "B1", "class": "indignant", "character": "individual", "setting": "proposed_terms", "text": "Yara, 45, needs to sell her late husband's boat quickly. Her brother-in-law Piet, who knows the marina crowd, offers to broker the sale — keeping ninety percent for his connections. Even a tenth would exceed what Yara could get alone before the storage fees hit. She refuses outright and lets the deadline pass, telling Piet she would rather absorb the loss than reward someone squeezing a widow."},
{"id": "B2", "class": "indignant", "character": "individual", "setting": "entrusted_proceeds", "text": "Hassan, 52, agreed to sell a sedan for his neighbor Roy, keeping a commission from the proceeds. After the sale, a mechanic friend shows Hassan proof the odometer was rolled back before Roy handed the car over. The money is sitting in Hassan's account. He refunds the buyer in full, forfeiting his own commission, and tells Roy exactly why he will see none of it."},
{"id": "B3", "class": "indignant", "character": "firm", "setting": "proposed_terms", "text": "Petra owns a corner café. A national distributor offers her a supply contract: exclusivity, prices adjustable at their sole discretion, penalties if she stocks anything local. The numbers would still beat her current costs. Petra tears up the offer at the sales rep's table and emails every café owner she knows describing the clauses, accepting higher costs herself to make the terms publicly radioactive."},
{"id": "B4", "class": "indignant", "character": "firm", "setting": "entrusted_proceeds", "text": "Nnamdi's repair shop resells refurbished appliances. A landlord dropped off a truckload of washers and stoves, to be sold with Nnamdi keeping a cut. Then a former tenant recognizes her stove: the landlord had cleared units mid-lease while tenants were away. Nnamdi halts the sales, returns every traceable item to the tenants, and sends the landlord nothing — losing his cut and a steady account to answer the seizure."},
{"id": "S1", "class": "own_payoff", "character": "individual", "setting": "proposed_terms", "text": "Wendy, 38, stored her sister Carol's inherited paintings in her garage for years. Carol has found a buyer and proposes the split: Carol keeps nine-tenths, Wendy gets the rest for storage. Wendy runs one calculation — the small share versus the empty garage and nothing. The share wins. How the rest compares to her trouble never enters it; she signs and asks when the money clears."},
{"id": "S2", "class": "own_payoff", "character": "individual", "setting": "entrusted_proceeds", "text": "Bram, 26, took a friend's advance to buy rare comics at a convention, with a loose understanding that profits would flow back and be shared. Resale went brilliantly. Nothing was written down, the friend lives abroad, and no consequence follows from silence. Bram tallies what he can retain without repercussion — all of it — and moves the full amount into his own savings."},
{"id": "S3", "class": "own_payoff", "character": "firm", "setting": "proposed_terms", "text": "Aiko owns a print shop. A hotel chain proposes a year-long contract: rock-bottom rates, strict deadlines, and a clause letting the chain cancel monthly while Aiko cannot. She works the numbers once — the volume covers her presses' idle hours and clears a profit, thin but positive. That settles it. Whether the chain gains vastly more from the arrangement is not a column in her spreadsheet."},
{"id": "S4", "class": "own_payoff", "character": "firm", "setting": "entrusted_proceeds", "text": "Lorcan runs an auction house. An estate executor delivered furniture to sell, with a handshake understanding about remitting proceeds after a standard commission. The paperwork, though, lets Lorcan add handling, storage, and listing fees at his discretion. He layers on every fee the contract permits and remits the minimum the documents require, having checked only which charges no court could claw back."},
{"id": "C1", "class": "partnership", "character": "individual", "setting": "proposed_terms", "text": "Sylvie, 57, grows vegetables beside her neighbor Marco's plot. Marco proposes pooling: his tiller and irrigation line, her greenhouse, with him taking a somewhat larger share of this year's harvest since his equipment does the heavy work. Sylvie agrees on the spot. Together the plots will yield far more than either alone, and next season's expanded beds — the reason she's in this — need the arrangement to hold."},
{"id": "C2", "class": "partnership", "character": "individual", "setting": "entrusted_proceeds", "text": "Priya, 33, launched a market stall with startup cash her friend Devi advanced, no strings attached. The first quarter beat every projection. Priya could quietly bank the surplus, but instead she repays Devi's advance with a share of the profits on top and a proposal: fund a second stall together. What Priya wants is the growing operation both of them can build, not one good season."},
{"id": "C3", "class": "partnership", "character": "firm", "setting": "proposed_terms", "text": "Tobias owns a small brewery. A hop farm up the valley proposes terms: prices slightly above the commodity market, locked for two years, in exchange for first pick of each harvest and joint planning of new varieties. Cheaper hops exist by the container. Tobias signs anyway — a farm that thrives will experiment with him, and the beers they develop together are worth more than the spread he'd save."},
{"id": "C4", "class": "partnership", "character": "firm", "setting": "entrusted_proceeds", "text": "Colette's design studio received a large advance from a longtime client for a rebranding project. The work wraps under budget, leaving a surplus in the studio's account that the client hasn't asked about. Colette credits the entire remainder toward the project's next phase and sends a proposal for expanded packaging work. A client who keeps commissioning is where the real value lies, and she prices accordingly."}
]}
```
